newsitem.title: UK: IBCA says gives Croatia BBB minus foreign currency.
newsitem.headline: IBCA says gives Croatia BBB minus foreign currency.

text.p: IBCA, the European credit rating agency, said on Friday it had assigned a BBB minus long-term foreign currency rating to Croatia.

"The rating is the first to be given to Croatia by IBCA and will apply to both the forthcoming Croatia Eurobond issue and to $1.5 billion of debt issued by the Republic to replace its part of the obligations of the former Republic of Yugoslavia," IBCA said in a statement.
"The rating will also act as a ceiling for IBCA rated banks and corporates in Croatia," IBCA said.

IBCA said it also assigned a short-term foreign currency rating of A3 for securities maturing within one year. It also awarded Croatia the long term local currency rating of A minus to cover some $2.9 billion of securities payable in kuna.

"The agency's investment grade rating for Croatia reflects the impressive macro-economic stabilisation with the lowest rate of inflation of the transistion economies, and the substantial export-earning capacity and potential of Croatia," IBCA said.
"There is a high level of education of the population, and the business community is relatively sophisticated by the standards of other transistion economies (except Slovenia)," IBCA said.
"Moreover, external debt is still modest compared with either GDP or foreign exhcange receipts," IBCA said.
IBCA said the national track record of national institutions is a constraint on the rating, but is less so than other contries emerging form federations.
IBCA said it believes that the risks of Croatia being embroiled in anther war are now small since the frontiers are now mutally recognised by Croatia, Bosnia and Yugoslavia.

"However, IBCA highlights the risk that tensions in Bosnia may taint Croatia by association and adversely affect both tourist earnings -- the potential jewel in Croatia's foreign currency earnings -- and the foreign direct investment which would help fund reconstruction," it said.
IBCA also said that the Croatian record on structural reform has been patchy, with slow progress notably on privatisation, it said.

"Within Croatia, both the substantial macro-economic consensus around sound financial policies in the main parties, and the strong desire to integrate within the European Union are likely to underpin both the democratic and the economic thrust of Croatia's reform efforts," IBCA said.
